children: The U.S. economy has seen strong growth and low unemployment for the last three years, but there's one worrying trend that has persisted – hiring is still fairly muted.
This "low-hire, low-fire" labor market largely continued in September, as seen in the latest Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics said the number of
was little changed in September, even as it reached a four-month high. Layoffs fell to their lowest level in a year and a half.
"Employers are hiring at the slowest pace since 2013, and workers are quitting at the slowest pace since 2015," Cory Stahle, economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab, noted after the JOLTS release.
"When so few people move, few jobs open up for anyone trying to get in, with new graduates and unemployed workers hit hardest," he added.
But this wasn't always the case. The U.S. added over 2M jobs almost every year in the decade before the COVID-19 pandemic.
More than 9M jobs were lost during the pandemic, after which the labor market staged a remarkable recovery – 14M jobs were added from 2021 to 2023.
However, in the years that followed, hiring slowed significantly while GDP kept growing, with the economy now in its sixth year of expansion.
Employers have added ~86,000 jobs on average per month this year, improving from last year's average of under 10,000.
And while the unemployment rate has held steady at above 4% in 2026, this doesn’t mean workers are finding jobs easily.

"Unemployment is low because job loss is near historical lows," researchers at Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City pointed out recently. "In a healthy labor market, low unemployment derives from both a relatively low job loss rate and a relatively high job finding rate. When low unemployment is driven by a low job loss rate alone, however, the labor market may be more fragile than it initially appears."
The researchers explained that if the job loss rate were to increase, the low job finding rate would leave little capacity to absorb displaced workers.

"The same increase in job loss would lead to a greater increase in the unemployment rate in the current labor market than it would in a more fluid labor market, where hires and fires are higher and worker churn is greater," they stated.
Latest nonfarm payrolls data has shown that hiring was
in October. The U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, well above economists' consensus estimate of 62,000.
The job growth numbers for the prior two months were also revised higher. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1% from September's 4.2%.
As these numbers are subject to revision, it's too early to say that the labor market is out of the low-hire, low-fire environment.
In a report released by Challenger, Gray & Christmas on Thursday, U.S.-based employers' layoff plans in October fell to the lowest level since 2023.

"This is a low-fire environment," Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas, said. "Employers are holding on to the workers they have heading into the holidays, and the hiring they are announcing is
, seasonal work. Companies want the flexibility to meet holiday demand without adding permanent headcount."
